It is. But here's the twist. When the bank said done, her new balance had not been saved anywhere permanent. Not yet.
So how can a bank promise something it hasn't saved? This happens every time you tap Pay. It takes a few milliseconds. Let's slow it right down.
Every computer works a lot like a restaurant kitchen. This one belongs to Priya's bank, and it's busy, even late at night.

The old card will need cleaning up later.
Now, the most important habit in this kitchen. It's the secret to the whole story.
Before any change counts, it must be written in the company notebook. Not the page itself, just a short note about the change.

Then the note itself: page 42, Priya, now 300, order 812.

Quick recap. Priya's new balance, 300, exists only in the fridge. One power cut, and it's gone. So how can the bank tell Priya done, right now?
Mira writes one final note: order 812, finished.
Here's the trick. She doesn't carry page 42 to the storeroom. A payment can touch pages all over the place, and there are thousands of them.
But the notes all sit together, on one notebook page. So she only sends the notebook. One small, quick trip.
She asks the Manager to save the notebook to disk.
And then she waits. Every payment you have ever made has waited for this one trip.
Two other chefs finish at the same moment. The Manager takes all their notes in the same trip. That's called group commit.
The notes are in the storeroom. Now, even if the lights go out, Priya's payment can be rebuilt from them.

Order 812 is finished, so Arjun wakes up. He sees the new 300, and adds his cashback on top: 400. His order is not finished yet.

Which is exactly where our story began.

Look inside the storeroom. Mira's notes are here. And page 42? Still says 500.
The 300 only ever lived in the fridge. And the fridge has just forgotten everything.
So, did the bank just lie to Priya?
When the power comes back, a recovery chef opens the notebook and replays every note, in order.
First, it fetches page 42 from the storeroom. It says 500.
Then it finds the full-page copy Mira made. Remember it? Page 42 comes back exactly as she left it: 300.
Order 812: done. Priya's money is safe. The notebook kept the promise.
And Arjun's cashback? It was never finished, and its note never reached the storeroom. So it simply never happened. His app tries again.
Now imagine the lights went out a moment earlier, while the Manager was still walking with the notebook.
Then Priya never hears done. Her app shows an error, her balance is still 500, and she simply taps Pay again.
No promise was made, so no promise was broken.
That's the whole secret. The bank only says done once the note about the change is safe in the storeroom.
Later that night, the clean-up crew arrives. Every few minutes, the Supervisor makes sure every changed page really gets carried to the storeroom.
What if the lights go out halfway through this delivery? Page 42 could land half old, half new. Torn. A short note can't fix that.
But the full-page copy can. That's exactly why Mira made it.
This time all goes well. Look at the score: page 42 is finally in the storeroom, saying 300.

This whole story rests on trust. When the Manager says it's in the storeroom, it has to be true. In 2018, engineers found that it wasn't always.
A delivery to the storeroom failed. The Manager reported the error, once.

Today, if this ever happens, PostgreSQL stops on purpose, restarts, and rebuilds everything from the notebook.
A promise is only as strong as the promises underneath it.

Since PostgreSQL 18, for big jobs like reading a whole table, PostgreSQL can ask for many pages ahead of time, and keep working while they arrive.
Deciding who gets a lamp next is the operating system's scheduler. It happens thousands of times a second.
The Manager gives her a private spot in the fridge that no other chef can open.

Keeping several versions of the same row like this is called MVCC. Readers never block writers, and writers never block readers.
